Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis of Year Established): Jewish Encyclopedia (Gottheil & Bacher) states Nehardea was the native city of the Jewish brothers Anilai and Asinai who 'in the first third of the first century C.E.' founded a robber-state on the Euphrates (midpoint of 1-33 CE = c. 17); it also quotes Josephus (Ant. 18.9.1) that the city 'is thickly populated' and that Nehardea and Nisibis were 'the treasuries of the Eastern Jews' for the Temple taxes. No number given. NOT counted as documented presence: the tradition (Sherira Gaon; Talmud) that Jehoiachin's exiles of 597 BCE founded the community and built the Shaf we-Yatib synagogue with earth and stones from Jerusalem (legend); and the JE claim that Hyrcanus II lived in Nehardea as a Parthian captive c. 40-36 BCE (Josephus Ant. 15.2.2 says only 'a habitation at Babylon, where there were Jews in great numbers'). Identification: adjacent to or identical with Anbar near Fallujah.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (via Jewish Virtual Library): the Jewish settlement was early; Jewish presence in the century before the destruction of the Temple (c. 30 BCE-70 CE; midpoint c. 20 CE) is attested by Josephus (Ant. 18.311-313): Babylonian Jews concentrated the half-shekel offering and Temple donations at walled Nehardea (protected by the Euphrates) and sent them to Jerusalem. A large organised community acting as regional collection centre; no count. EJ also records the tradition of Jehoiachin-era settlers (legend, not counted).

Josephus Ant. 18.310-313 (Posen Library translation and commentary): Nehardea 'not only a well-populated' city with extensive territory, defended by the Euphrates and walls; Jews deposited the half-shekel and other Temple offerings there; 'many myriads of men' escorted the donations to Jerusalem for fear of Parthian robbers - an ancient convoy/pilgrim figure for Babylonian Jewry as a whole, NOT the resident population of Nehardea, so Population blank. Dated c. 24 CE (c.) = midpoint of reign of Artabanus II (r. 10/11-38 CE), in whose time the account is set. Posen commentary: the account is novelistic and its historicity hard to determine.

Hayadan article (Hebrew; author a student of S. Safrai): the brothers Hasinai and Hanilai, natives of Nehardea, led a rebellion in Babylonia 'between the years 26 and 36 CE', outbreak dated 26 CE; 'many young men' (poor Jewish youths) joined them - no count. Notes that Josephus is the single ('orphan') source and some scholars doubt the story's reliability. The article also repeats Josephus that 'tens of thousands' took part in shipping the Temple money (convoy figure, not population).

Josephus Ant. 18.369-371 (Harland translation): after Anilaios' raids on Babylonian villages, the Babylonians 'sent ambassadors to Nearda to the Judeans there and demanded Anilaios'; the Judeans refused; after Anilaios was killed the Babylonians attacked the Judeans, who, unable to fight or live with them, moved to Seleucia (Harland: 'Judeans from Nearda resettle... at Seleukeia'). Confirms an organised Jewish community at Nehardea able to negotiate collectively; no count and no statement that none remained. Year c. 60 per Harland's chronology (brothers' rise c. 40 CE, 15 years, disasters c. 55-56, Seleucia massacre in the sixth year c. 66); other scholars (e.g. JE, Wikipedia) date the brothers c. 18-35 CE and these events to the later 30s CE. Harland stresses Josephus is the only source.

Josephus Ant. 18.372-379 (Posen Library translation): after the massacre of Jews at Seleucia ('more than fifty thousand men' slain - an ancient casualty figure for Seleucia, not Nehardea) and further hostility at Ctesiphon, 'most of them [the Jews] gathered themselves together and went to Nehardea and Nisibis and obtained security there by the strength of those cities', whose 'inhabitants, who were a great many, were all warlike men'. Refugee influx into an already large Jewish city; no count. Dated c. 65 CE per Posen's bracket ('in the sixth year [ca. 65 CE]'); traditional chronology (Neusner) places the Seleucia massacre c. 40 CE.
